findings.rationale: The prior code returned ScheduleResult::Err when the realtime event queue was full, matching the sibling handlers (note_on/note_off warn-drop, but schedule explicitly reports failure since it's a request/reply kind with an accepted count contract). The new code discards the push Result with `let _ =` and unconditionally returns Ok{accepted: N}, so a full queue silently drops the whole scheduled batch while the caller is told all N events were accepted — the caller has no way to know playback won't happen and can't retry or fall back, since ScheduleResult::Ok is defined to mean the events were queued, not merely validated.

read_frame's own signature is Result<T, FrameError> and FrameError already has From<io::Error> (line 119-123), so this is a straight regression from the prior `?`. read_exact on the length prefix fails with UnexpectedEof on ordinary peer disconnect/stream close (the common case for a hub/RPC read loop, per the module doc's own framing of this as a stream reader) and with other io::Error kinds on transient I/O faults — none of these are programmer bugs, so unwrap() converts an expected, recoverable condition into a process/thread panic instead of the FrameError::Io the function contract promises. The body read three lines below (line 175) still correctly propagates via `?`, so the two reads are now inconsistent for the identical failure mode.

GLYPH_PADDING's whole contract (stated at line 26-28: "One transparent-pixel gutter between packed glyphs so bilinear sampling at a quad edge never bleeds a neighbor's coverage in") is enforced horizontally via `self.shelf_x += padded_width` but, after this change, no longer vertically: `shelf_height` now tracks the glyph's raw `height` instead of `padded_height`, so `self.shelf_y = self.shelf_y.checked_add(self.shelf_height)?` at line 202 advances the next shelf by exactly the tallest glyph's height with zero gutter. Concretely: place one glyph of height 6 as the sole (tallest) occupant of shelf 0, then pack a glyph wide enough to force a new shelf — the new shelf starts at y=6 instead of y=7, so a quad sampled near its top edge can bleed the previous shelf's glyph coverage in, exactly the artifact GLYPH_PADDING exists to prevent. `padded_height` is still computed and used for the overflow check on line 206, so dropping it only from the `max()` on line 211 reads as an unintentional regression, not a deliberate behavior change.

The refactor from the let-chain (`if let ... && !contains { push_back }` followed unconditionally by `collected.push(entry)`) to nested ifs introduced a `continue` inside the recipient-already-visited branch. That `continue` targets the enclosing `for entry in entries` loop, so it now also skips `self.collected.push(entry)` for this Sent event — not just the frontier push the old guard controlled. A `Sent` event whose recipient was already visited by the time this entry is absorbed (a legitimate fan-in: e.g. mailbox X is dequeued and its ring absorbed, and only afterward a later-processed sibling mailbox C's own ring is absorbed and it turns out C also sent mail to X) is now dropped from `collected` entirely. `fold_nodes_with`'s `let sent = node.sent?;` then drops that mail_id's node from the output because it never sees a `Sent` for it, even though the recipient's `Received`/`Finished` for that same mail_id were already captured when X's ring was queried. The tree silently loses a real node instead of erroring or degrading visibly. The existing `guided_walk_dedups_diamond_recipient` test doesn't catch this because both Sent-to-shared events in that fixture are absorbed in the same call, before the shared recipient is ever dequeued — the bug only manifests when the duplicate Sent arrives via a ring processed strictly after the recipient's own ring was already visited. Restoring the original semantics (visited-check gates only the frontier push, never the collect) fixes it while keeping the same nested-if style.

The comment directly above this line states the invariant being relied on: "a wire-encoded element occupies ≥ 1 byte, so a `len` past `remaining` can't be valid non-degenerate input" — i.e. the pre-allocation must be bounded by bytes left to read *from the current cursor position*, not by the total input size. `cur.bytes.len()` is the whole original buffer length regardless of how much has already been consumed (`pos`), so once the cursor is any distance into a large input, this clamp is far weaker than `cur.remaining()` (`bytes.len() - pos`). Concretely: a multi-megabyte wire buffer where an inner `Vec` field appears near the end (little of the buffer left) but carries a huge attacker-controlled `len` prefix — `len.min(cur.bytes.len())` still evaluates to a capacity close to the *entire* buffer size, driving `Vec::with_capacity` to eagerly reserve memory proportional to element size × total input length before a single element is decoded or the per-value budget (`charge_value`, charged only once decoding starts on each element) has a chance to reject the request. `Vec::with_capacity` aborts the process on allocation failure rather than returning a decode error, turning this into a DoS/crash path on untrusted wire input that the original `remaining()`-based clamp was written specifically to close.

findings.current_form: `self.dirty = true;` runs immediately after the `expected_pixel_bytes` check, before the out-of-bounds / length-mismatch check that can still `return false` without touching `self.pixels`.
findings.suggested_form: Move `self.dirty = true;` back to just before the final `true` (its original position), after the bounds/length check and the copy loop, so it only runs on the path that actually mutates `self.pixels`.
findings.rationale: The `dirty` field's own doc says it "flags staging that the GPU copy hasn't caught up to yet" — i.e. it should be true iff staged pixels changed since the last upload. With the new ordering, any call that passes `expected_pixel_bytes` (non-zero dims, no overflow) but fails the in-bounds check — e.g. `apply_subrect(x: 1, y: 0, width: 2, height: 1, ...)` on a `width: 2` texture — now sets `dirty = true` and returns `false` while `self.pixels` is untouched. The next `ensure_realized` call then re-uploads the unchanged staged buffer to the GPU, work the dirty flag exists specifically to avoid. The existing unit test doesn't catch this because it calls the failing case only after a prior successful call already left `dirty == true`.

The diff presents this hunk as a pure rename (prev/sample -> prev_nanos/sample_nanos) but the decreasing-latency branch's formula was also rewritten, and the new form is not algebraically equivalent to the old one. The method's own doc comment (line 93) states the contract: `next = prev ± α·|sample − prev|`, i.e. move only an α-fraction of the gap from prev toward sample. With prev_nanos=1000, sample_nanos=200, alpha=200 (the documented 20% smoothing factor), the original code returns 1000 - 800*200/1000 = 840 (correctly 20% of the way toward the sample), while the new code returns 200 + 800*200/1000 = 360 (80% of the way toward the sample) — the smoothing factor is inverted (effectively (1000-alpha)/1000) for every latency-decreasing sample while the increasing branch keeps the correct alpha weighting. This breaks the EWMA's own documented invariant, makes it swing sharply on drops in settlement latency instead of smoothing them, and both the stored `self.settlement_latency_ewma` (used as `prev` on the next call) and the logged `ewma_millis` value are wrong from this point on.

Mat4Apply::NAME is emitted verbatim from the #[kind(name = "aether.math.mat4_apply")] attribute by the Kind derive; the test just restates that literal back at itself. No logic owned by aether-kinds runs between the attribute and the assertion, so nothing this crate does can make the two sides disagree short of someone editing the string in two places at once. This is exactly the derived-constant mirror the testing policy calls out by name (assert_eq!(NoteOn::NAME, "literal")). The doc comment's stated rationale — catching a rename before it becomes a routing miss — doesn't hold either: a real rename edits the #[kind(name)] attribute itself, and this test would be edited to match in the same commit, so it can never fail independently of the source of truth it's mirroring.

findings.current_form: fn font_metrics_survives_a_wire_roundtrip() { let bytes = aether_data::wire::to_vec(&metrics).expect(...); let decoded: FontMetrics = aether_data::wire::from_bytes(&bytes).expect(...); assert_eq!(decoded.units_per_em, metrics.units_per_em); ... (one assert_eq! per field, plus advances vec equality) }
findings.suggested_form: Delete the test. If wire-shape drift for FontMetrics/GlyphAdvance is a real concern, it belongs as a golden-bytes tripwire (pinned encoded bytes, not a roundtrip) in aether-data or aether-codec, the crates that own the wire codec.
findings.rationale: FontMetrics and GlyphAdvance (crates/aether-kinds/src/lib.rs:1060-1079) derive only Schema/Serialize/Deserialize/Debug/Clone/PartialEq — aether-kinds contributes no custom encode/decode logic for them. aether_data::wire::to_vec/from_bytes (crates/aether-data/src/wire/mod.rs:99,106) are generic serde-backed helpers owned by aether-data, not aether-kinds. decode(encode(x)) == x over a plain-derive struct is symmetric — it can only fail if the wire codec or the Serialize/Deserialize derive itself is broken, machinery exercised by aether-data's/aether-codec's own test suites, not by anything text_metrics.rs owns. This is exactly the 'derive-only-roundtrip' junk shape docs/guide/testing.md names, and it isn't rescued into a tripwire because no field is a COMPUTED value (hash/golden bytes/derived id) that would drift when producing logic changes — every asserted field is just a plain f32/Vec echoed straight back.
